title: Search Open Websites/Domains
summary: This technique describes open source collection from public websites and domains, where the adversary never touches victim infrastructure. Social profiles, press releases, tender portals, conference agendas, support forums and job adverts are mined for organisational structure, technology choices, supplier relationships and named staff. The output feeds later stages: a believable pretext for phishing, a target list for account creation, or a supplier relationship worth abusing for trusted access. The mechanism is ordinary web browsing, and in most cases the requests land on third party servers rather than the victim, which is why there is often no victim side telemetry at all. Where logs do exist, they show automated retrieval of many pages in a short window from a single source, or crawling of a corporate site by an unexpected client. The distinction a defender must hold on to is that legitimate market research, journalists and candidates generate similar patterns, so intent must be inferred from correlation with later activity such as credential phishing or account registration rather than from the browsing alone.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker reads information that is already public on websites. They look at social media, news pages, job adverts and company sites. They collect facts about your organisation without contacting you at all.
beginner.whyItMatters: Public posts often reveal names, roles, tools and suppliers. Attackers use these facts to write messages that sound genuine. Because the reading happens on other companies' websites, your own logs may show nothing. It is quiet, cheap and legal, which makes it popular.
howItWorks: The attacker starts with your main website and reads pages about services, staff and partners.
They check job adverts, which often name the exact systems and software you run.
They review social media posts for names, roles, locations and internal events.
They look at news articles and tender notices for growth, mergers and new technology projects.
They combine the pieces into a profile of who to contact and what to say.
They keep the profile for later, such as a phishing email that mentions a real project.
beginner.example: Think of a busy market where traders chat loudly about their stock and their plans. A stranger can walk around all day, listen carefully and learn everything about the stalls. Nobody was robbed, but the stranger now knows exactly who has the most to lose and who leaves their stall unattended.
takeaways: Anything you publish can be read, stored and reused against you years later.
Job adverts are a rich source of detail about your internal technology stack.
You cannot stop this reading, but you can limit what you reveal and watch for impersonation.

objectives: Explain what open source reconnaissance is and why it needs no contact with the victim.
Identify the public sources that most often expose useful organisational detail.
Describe how collected facts support phishing and account based attacks.
Explain why victim side logging frequently shows nothing for this technique.
Suggest realistic controls that reduce the value of published information.
